claim: Phycobilisome (PBS) is the main light-harvesting antenna in cyanobacteria and red algae.
source: Phycobilisome (PBS) is the main light-harvesting antenna in cyanobacteria and red algae.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the function of PBS in these organisms.

claim: The in situ structure of the PBS–PSII supercomplex from Porphyridium purpureum UTEX 2757 was determined using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging.
source: Here we report the in situ structure of the PBS–PSII supercomplex from Porphyridium purpureum UTEX 2757 using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used to determine the structure.

claim: Each PBS interacts with six PSII monomers in the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
source: In the PBS–PSII supercomplex, each PBS interacts with six PSII monomers, of which four directly bind to the PBS, and two bind indirectly.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four PSII monomers directly bind to the PBS and two bind indirectly in the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
source: In the PBS–PSII supercomplex, each PBS interacts with six PSII monomers, of which four directly bind to the PBS, and two bind indirectly.
evidence: This describes the binding pattern observed in the structure.

claim: Three 'connector' proteins contribute to the connections between PBS and PSIIs.
source: Additional three 'connector' proteins also contribute to the connections between PBS and PSIIs.
evidence: The manuscript identifies three unassigned connector proteins in the structure.

claim: Two PsbO subunits from adjacent PSII dimers bind with each other.
source: Two PsbO subunits from adjacent PSII dimers bind with each other, which may promote stabilization of the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: The binding of two PsbO subunits from adjacent PSII dimers may promote stabilization of the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
source: Two PsbO subunits from adjacent PSII dimers bind with each other, which may promote stabilization of the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: αLCM connects with CP43 of PSII monomer.
source: By analyzing the interaction interface between PBS and PSII, we reveal that αLCM and ApcD connect with CP43 of PSII monomer and that αLCM also interacts with CP47' of the neighboring PSII monomer, suggesting the multiple light energy delivery pathways.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the interaction interfaces in the structure.

claim: ApcD connects with CP43 of PSII monomer.
source: By analyzing the interaction interface between PBS and PSII, we reveal that αLCM and ApcD connect with CP43 of PSII monomer and that αLCM also interacts with CP47' of the neighboring PSII monomer, suggesting the multiple light energy delivery pathways.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the interaction interfaces in the structure.

claim: αLCM interacts with CP47' of the neighboring PSII monomer.
source: By analyzing the interaction interface between PBS and PSII, we reveal that αLCM and ApcD connect with CP43 of PSII monomer and that αLCM also interacts with CP47' of the neighboring PSII monomer, suggesting the multiple light energy delivery pathways.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the interaction interfaces in the structure.

claim: The connections between αLCM, ApcD, and PSII subunits suggest multiple light energy delivery pathways.
source: By analyzing the interaction interface between PBS and PSII, we reveal that αLCM and ApcD connect with CP43 of PSII monomer and that αLCM also interacts with CP47' of the neighboring PSII monomer, suggesting the multiple light energy delivery pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structural connections.

claim: Red algae living in deep water can efficiently use dim and green light that cannot be absorbed by plants.
source: Red algae living in deep water can efficiently use dim and green light that cannot be absorbed by plants (Tschudy, 1934).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PBS is located on the stromal surface of the thylakoid membrane and captures light energy.
source: The primary light-harvesting antenna is the phycobilisome (PBS), which is located on the stromal surface of the thylakoid membrane and captures light energy (Gantt and Conti, 1965; Gantt and Conti, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PBS mainly transfers the light energy to PSII, leading to water splitting.
source: PBS mainly transfers the light energy to PSII, leading to water splitting (Biggins and Bruce, 1989; Ley and Butler, 1977a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PBS could also directly couple with PSI.
source: PBS could also directly couple with PSI (Mullineaux, 1992; Su et al., 1992; Kondo et al., 2007; Ueno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PBSs are composed of chromophore-bearing phycobiliproteins (PBPs) and linker proteins, which further assemble into central core and peripheral rods.
source: PBSs are composed of chromophore-bearing phycobiliproteins (PBPs) and linker proteins, which further assemble into central core and peripheral rods (Gantt et al., 1976; Zilinskas and Greenwald, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of PBS from red algae has been determined at resolutions of 3.5 Å and 2.82 Å.
source: Recently, the cryo-electron microscope (cryo-EM) structures of PBS from red algae at resolutions of 3.5 Å (Zhang et al., 2017) and 2.82 Å (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The PBS in Porphyridium purpureum consists of a tricylindrical PBS core, 14 rods, 8 individual extra PE hexamers, and 24 individual extra PE α or β subunits.
source: The cryo-EM structure of PBS in red alga Porphyridium purpureum (Ma et al., 2020) shows that the PBS consists of a tricylindrical PBS core, 14 rods (Rod a–Rod g, Rod a'–Rod g'), 8 individual extra PE (αβ)6 hexamers (Ha–Hd, Ha'–Hd'), and 24 individual extra PE α or β subunits.
evidence: This is based on a previous cryo-EM structure cited in the manuscript.

claim: The PBS core contains one top cylinder B composed of two allophycocyanin (APC) (αβ)3 trimers, and two bottom cylinders each assembled by three APC trimers.
source: The core contains one top cylinder B, composed of two allophycocyanin (APC) (αβ)3 trimers, and two bottom cylinders (A and A'), each of which is assembled by three APC trimers (A1–A3, A2 and A3 form APC hexamer).
evidence: This describes the structural composition of the PBS core based on previous work.

claim: The rods consist of phycoerythrin (PE) and phycocyanin (PC) hexamers or only PE hexamers.
source: The rods consist of phycoerythrin (PE) and phycocyanin (PC) hexamers or only PE hexamers.
evidence: This describes the composition of PBS rods based on established knowledge.

claim: Energy absorbed by Rod transfers unidirectionally from the distal PE to the basal PC, and then funnels to APC in the core, and eventually to the two terminal emitters.
source: Thus, the energy absorbed by Rod transfers unidirectionally from the distal PE to the basal PC, and then funnels to APC in the core, and eventually to the two terminal emitters, including chromophores in the core–membrane linker protein (LCM, also called ApcE) (Capuano et al., 1991; Lundell et al., 1981; Tang et al., 2015) and allophycocyanin D (ApcD) (Glazer and Bryant, 1975; Peng et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the energy transfer pathway supported by citations.

claim: The two terminal emitters in PBS include chromophores in the core–membrane linker protein (LCM, also called ApcE) and allophycocyanin D (ApcD).
source: Thus, the energy absorbed by Rod transfers unidirectionally from the distal PE to the basal PC, and then funnels to APC in the core, and eventually to the two terminal emitters, including chromophores in the core–membrane linker protein (LCM, also called ApcE) (Capuano et al., 1991; Lundell et al., 1981; Tang et al., 2015) and allophycocyanin D (ApcD) (Glazer and Bryant, 1975; Peng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PSII is a multi-pigment transmembrane protein complex involved in converting light energy into electrochemical potential energy.
source: PSII is a multi-pigment transmembrane protein complex involved in converting light energy into electrochemical potential energy (Adachi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: X-ray crystal structures of PSII from red alga Cyanidium caldarium, cyanobacterium Thermosynechococcus elongatus, and cryo-EM structures from various organisms have been determined.
source: The X-ray crystal structures of PSII from red alga Cyanidium caldarium (Ago et al., 2016), cyanobacterium Thermosynechococcus elongatus (Nakajima et al., 2018), and the cryo-EM structure of PSII from green alga Chlamydomonas reihardtii (Sheng et al., 2019), the marine diatom Chaetoceros gracilis (Pi et al., 2019), and the higher plants Arabidopsis thaliana (van Bezouwen et al., 2017), Spinacia oleracea (Wei et al., 2016), and Pisum sativum (Su et al., 2017) have revealed the structural basis of energy transfer, electron transfer, and photoprotection within the photosystem.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The main subunits of PSII include the reaction center D1, D2 protein, and chlorophyll-a binding proteins, CP43 and CP47.
source: The main subunits of PSII include the reaction center D1, D2 protein, and chlorophyll-a binding proteins, CP43 and CP47.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSII structure.

claim: Both CP43 and CP47 subunits have been reported to mediate the energy transfer from PBS to the reaction center.
source: Both CP43 and CP47 subunits have been reported to mediate the energy transfer from PBS to the reaction center (Ueno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PBSs in red algae are tightly arranged in ordered rows on the thylakoid in most regions and randomly packed in some areas.
source: PBSs in red algae are tightly arranged in ordered rows on the thylakoid in most regions and randomly packed in some areas (Arteni et al., 2008; Lange et al., 1990; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous microscopy studies.

claim: PBS arrangement in the two regions is dynamically regulated, varying with the cell's age, the supply of nutrients, and available light.
source: PBS arrangement in the two regions is dynamically regulated, varying with the cell's age, the supply of nutrients, and available light (Arteni et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Sagert and Schubert, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The stoichiometric ratio of PBS/PSII in red algae and cyanobacteria remains controversial, ranging from 1:1 to 1:4.
source: However, the stoichiometric ratio of PBS/PSII in red algae and cyanobacteria remains controversial, ranging from 1:1 to 1:4 (Arteni et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 1989; Ohki et al., 1987; Takahashi et al., 2009), which likely reflects different growth conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing different ratios.

claim: Different approaches showed that PBS connects with PSII through ApcD, αLCM, and ApcF.
source: Different approaches showed that PBS connects with PSII through ApcD, αLCM (the α domain of LCM), and ApcF (Zhao et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ApcD and αLCM are well known as terminal emitters for mediating the transfer of energy from PBS to PSII.
source: In particular, ApcD and αLCM are well known as terminal emitters for mediating the transfer of energy from PBS to PSII.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The negative staining structure of the purified PBS–PSII supercomplex in Anabaena sp. strain PCC 7120 proposed that αLCM and ApcF of PBS play important roles in mediating PBS interaction with PSII.
source: The negative staining structure of the purified PBS–PSII supercomplex in the Anabaena sp. strain PCC 7120 proposed that αLCM and ApcF of PBS play important roles in mediating PBS interaction with PSII (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The cross-linking structure of the purified PBS–PSII–PSI megacomplex in Synechocystis PCC 6803 identified five interlinks associated with αLCM and PSII.
source: The cross-linking structure of the purified PBS–PSII–PSI megacomplex in the cyanobacteria Synechocystis PCC 6803 identified five interlinks associated with αLCM and PSII (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous cross-linking study.

claim: In situ cryo-ET in combination with cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling is currently a powerful approach for directly dissecting macromolecular structures in the unperturbed cellular environment at molecular resolution.
source: In situ cryo-ET in combination with cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling is currently a powerful approach for directly dissecting macromolecular structures in the unperturbed cellular environment at molecular resolution (Wagner et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological papers.

claim: The native PBS–PSII supercomplex was identified at a resolution of 14.3 Å.
source: Here, by using this approach, we identified the native PBS–PSII supercomplex and the double PBS–PSII supercomplex containing two adjacent PBS–PSII supercomplexes at resolutions of 14.3 Å and 15.6 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the resolution achieved in the study.

claim: The double PBS–PSII supercomplex containing two adjacent PBS–PSII supercomplexes was identified at a resolution of 15.6 Å.
source: Here, by using this approach, we identified the native PBS–PSII supercomplex and the double PBS–PSII supercomplex containing two adjacent PBS–PSII supercomplexes at resolutions of 14.3 Å and 15.6 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the resolution achieved in the study.

claim: P. purpureum was cultured under low-light conditions to mimic its natural habitat and to increase the population of regularly distributed PBS–PSII supercomplexes.
source: The red alga, P. purpureum, was cultured under low-light conditions to mimic its natural habitat (Cunningham et al., 1989) and to increase the population of regularly distributed PBS–PSII supercomplexes (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used, supported by citations.

claim: Cells were harvested in the exponential phase of growth and were immediately vitrified on cryo-EM grids to minimize environmental affection.
source: Cells were harvested in the exponential phase of growth and were immediately vitrified on cryo-EM grids to minimize environmental affection (Kaňa et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, supported by a citation.

claim: Most PBS–PSII supercomplexes are packed in an orderly fashion on the thylakoid membranes.
source: The tomogram slice shows that most PBS–PSII supercomplexes are packed in an orderly fashion on the thylakoid membranes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the tomogram data.

claim: PBSs are sandwiched between parallel thylakoid membranes.
source: Consistent with the conventional transmission electron microscope ultrastructures of other red algae (Gantt and Conti, 1965; Gantt et al., 1968; Tsekos et al., 1996; Wanner and Kost, 1980), PBSs are sandwiched between parallel thylakoid membranes.
evidence: This observation is consistent with previous electron microscopy studies.

claim: Adjacent PBSs were attached to the upper and lower thylakoid membrane in opposite directions.
source: In the cross-section view, adjacent PBSs were attached to the upper and lower thylakoid membrane in opposite directions (Figure 1A,B,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the tomogram data.

claim: Opposite PBSs are stacked into linear rows.
source: In the two orthogonal views, opposite PBSs are stacked into linear rows respectively (Figure 1C,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C, Video 1, Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the tomogram data.

claim: PBS rows are arranged in parallel, forming a large two-dimensional pattern covering the thylakoid membrane.
source: These PBS rows are arranged in parallel, forming a large two-dimensional pattern covering the thylakoid membrane.
evidence: This is an observation from the tomogram data.

claim: Densities evident at the bottom of PBSs are embedded within the thylakoid membrane and represent PSIIs.
source: In the cross-section view, densities are evident at the bottom of PBSs, which are embedded within the thylakoid membrane. Protrusions are visible on the luminal side (Figure 1A). The features of these densities are consistent with the location and morphology of PSIIs (Ago et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2015; Lange et al., 1990). From this, we can infer that these represent PSIIs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphology and location of densities in the tomogram.

claim: The 2.82 Å single-particle PBS structure was well-fitted into the sub-tomogram map.
source: The recently determined 2.82 Å single-particle PBS (PDB code 6 KGX) (Ma et al., 2020) was well-fitted into our sub-tomogram map (Supplementary file 1), except for the individual extra PE β subunit between the Rod e and Rod d' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the fitting of a previous structure into the current data.

claim: The individual extra PE β subunit between Rod e and Rod d' did not fit well into the sub-tomogram map.
source: The recently determined 2.82 Å single-particle PBS (PDB code 6 KGX) (Ma et al., 2020) was well-fitted into our sub-tomogram map (Supplementary file 1), except for the individual extra PE β subunit between the Rod e and Rod d' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This describes a discrepancy between the previous structure and the current data.

claim: The map's slice view shows a similar PSII dimer array structure resembling that of the red algae Porphyridium cruentum.
source: The map's slice view shows a similar PSII dimer array structure resembling that of the red algae Porphyridium cruentum (Lange et al., 1990; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study.

claim: PSII from the red algae C. caldarium is evolutionarily most similar to P. purpureum.
source: PSII from the red algae C. caldarium (PDB code 4YUU) (Ago et al., 2016) is, evolutionarily, most similar to P. purpureum, and almost all the subunits show high homogeneity (ranging from 35% to 100%) with that of P. purpureum (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and sequence comparison.

claim: Almost all the subunits of PSII from C. caldarium show high homogeneity (ranging from 35% to 100%) with that of P. purpureum.
source: PSII from the red algae C. caldarium (PDB code 4YUU) (Ago et al., 2016) is, evolutionarily, most similar to P. purpureum, and almost all the subunits show high homogeneity (ranging from 35% to 100%) with that of P. purpureum (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: The X-ray model of PSII from C. caldarium shows a high cross-correlation coefficient (all above 80%) with the sub-tomogram map.
source: We then docked the X-ray model of PSII from C. caldarium into the sub-tomogram map, which shows a high cross-correlation coefficient (all above 80%) between the model and sub-tomogram map (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the quality of the model fitting.

claim: In the sub-tomogram map, two PBSs interact with a linear array of PSII dimers.
source: In the sub-tomogram map, two PBSs (labeled as PBS1 and PBS2) interact with a linear array of PSII dimers (labeled as A, B, C, A', B', C', C", Figure 2A (left panel), Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the sub-tomogram map.

claim: The PBS/PSII ratio is 1:6 in the linear array.
source: In this array, the PBS/PSII ratio is 1:6, that is, one PBS with six associated monomeric PSIIs periodically repeated along with the linear array.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the structure.

claim: Each PBS is directly anchored to a pair of PSIIs dimers.
source: In the double PBS–PSII map, each PBS is directly anchored to a pair of PSIIs dimers, i.e., PBS1 on the A–B pair and PBS2 on the A'–B' pair (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the sub-tomogram map.

claim: The C' dimer connects the A–B pair to the A'–B' pair.
source: The C' dimer connects the A–B pair to the A'–B' pair, while the two PSIIs in the C' dimer respectively interact with the lateral disc-like densities on both sides of PBS, which have features of PBS hexamer (discussed later), and thus indirectly attach to PBS1 and PBS2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the sub-tomogram map.

claim: The two PSIIs in the C' dimer respectively interact with the lateral disc-like densities on both sides of PBS and thus indirectly attach to PBS1 and PBS2.
source: The C' dimer connects the A–B pair to the A'–B' pair, while the two PSIIs in the C' dimer respectively interact with the lateral disc-like densities on both sides of PBS, which have features of PBS hexamer (discussed later), and thus indirectly attach to PBS1 and PBS2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the sub-tomogram map.

claim: The distance between the PSII dimers A and B is approximately 12.4 nm.
source: The distance between the PSII dimers A and B is approximately 12.4 nm, and the face planes of the two PSII dimers make a lateral angle of approximately 14° with the plane of the PBS central core.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure.

claim: The face planes of the two PSII dimers make a lateral angle of approximately 14° with the plane of the PBS central core.
source: The distance between the PSII dimers A and B is approximately 12.4 nm, and the face planes of the two PSII dimers make a lateral angle of approximately 14° with the plane of the PBS central core.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure.

claim: The centers of the two PSII double dimers shift approximately 3 nm along the plane of the PBS central core.
source: The centers of the two PSII double dimers shift approximately 3 nm along the plane of the PBS central core, which makes the twofold symmetry axes of PBS and 6 PSIIs coincide (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure.

claim: The twofold symmetry axes of PBS and 6 PSIIs coincide due to the 3 nm shift of PSII dimers.
source: The centers of the two PSII double dimers shift approximately 3 nm along the plane of the PBS central core, which makes the twofold symmetry axes of PBS and 6 PSIIs coincide (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural measurements.

claim: PSII dimers A and B bind with each other through a rigid density contributed by two adjacent PsbO subunits.
source: The improved PBS–PSII structure enables us to confirm that PSII dimers A and B bind with each other through a rigid density. By analyzing the fitting results, we suppose the density is most likely contributed by the two adjacent PsbO subunits: one is from the PSII monomer 1 of the PSII dimer A and the other from the PSII monomer 4 of the PSII dimer B (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density in the structure.

claim: The current resolution limits the ability to exclude that other factors may contribute to the density between PSII dimers A and B.
source: However, we are limited by the current resolution and could not exclude that other factors may contribute to the density.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: PsbO protein is found in PSII of all oxygenic organisms ranging from cyanobacteria and red algae to higher plants.
source: The PsbO protein is found in PSII of all oxygenic organisms ranging from cyanobacteria and red algae to higher plants and serves as the manganese-stabilizing protein directly involved in the stability of photosynthetic water-oxidizing complex (Ifuku and Noguchi, 2016; Popelkova and Yocum, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PsbO serves as the manganese-stabilizing protein directly involved in the stability of photosynthetic water-oxidizing complex.
source: The PsbO protein is found in PSII of all oxygenic organisms ranging from cyanobacteria and red algae to higher plants and serves as the manganese-stabilizing protein directly involved in the stability of photosynthetic water-oxidizing complex (Ifuku and Noguchi, 2016; Popelkova and Yocum, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PsbO could play an additional role in stabilizing adjacent PSII dimers in PSII dimer rows.
source: Our results suggest that PsbO could play an additional role in stabilizing adjacent PSII dimers in PSII dimer rows.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: The resolution of the PBS–PSII supercomplex was improved to 13.2 Å after post-processing from the 14.3 Å resolution map.
source: To analyze the lateral densities on both sides of PBS connecting PBS to PSII dimer C, we further improved the resolution of the PBS–PSII supercomplex to 13.2 Å after post-processing from the 14.3 Å resolution map (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes the data processing and resolution improvement.

claim: The lateral densities are round discs with solid densities in the center.
source: The slice view of the PBS–PSII map shows that the densities are round discs with solid densities in the center (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E–G).
evidence: This is an observation from the slice view of the map.

claim: The lateral densities are of the same size and shape as the extra hexamer found in the single-particle cryo-EM structure of P. purpureum PBS.
source: These features are reminiscent of the structure of the extra hexamer found in the single-particle cryo-EM structure of P. purpureum PBS. Moreover, the lateral densities are of the same size and shape as the extra hexamer.
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous structure.

claim: The lateral density could be contributed by a PE hexamer.
source: As all eight extra hexamers in P. purpureum PBS are PE hexamers, we hypothesize that the lateral density could be contributed by a PE hexamer, which is referred to as the lateral hexamer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural features and previous knowledge.

claim: The lateral hexamer connects with the bottom hexamer of Rod a and the second hexamer of Rod e.
source: Further analysis indicated that the lateral hexamer connects with the bottom hexamer of Rod a and the second hexamer of Rod e, which are the PC and PE hexamers, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: Extensive interfaces between PBS core and PSII are observed in the PBS–PSII map.
source: In the PBS–PSII map, extensive interfaces between PBS core and PSII are observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: There is a wide interface between αLCM and CP43 of PSII dimer A1.
source: As was shown in the proximal and middle clip views, there is a wide interface between αLCM and CP43 of PSII dimer A1 (CP43A1), as well as a relatively small interface between αLCM and CP47 of PSII dimer B1 (CP47B1) (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the surface clip views of the structure.

claim: There is a relatively small interface between αLCM and CP47 of PSII dimer B1.
source: As was shown in the proximal and middle clip views, there is a wide interface between αLCM and CP43 of PSII dimer A1 (CP43A1), as well as a relatively small interface between αLCM and CP47 of PSII dimer B1 (CP47B1) (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the surface clip views of the structure.

claim: The interactions between αLCM with CP43 and CP47 are consistent with the energy transfer from PBS to CP43 and CP47 detected in red algae and cyanobacteria.
source: These observations suggested the interactions between αLCM with CP43 and CP47, consistent with the energy transfer from PBS to CP43 and CP47 detected in red algae and cyanobacteria (Ueno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and previous research.

claim: The different sizes of the interface may provide a structural view that energy transfer from PBS to CP43 is the main pathway in red alga.
source: The different sizes of the interface may provide a structural view that energy transfer from PBS to CP43 is the main pathway in red alga (Ueno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: ApcD was involved in energy transfer from PBS to PSII.
source: The other terminal emitter subunit ApcD was also involved in energy transfer from PBS to PSII (Ashby and Mullineaux, 1999; Calzadilla et al., 2019; Ley and Butler, 1977b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is an interaction interface between ApcD and CP43A1.
source: The middle and distal clip views showed an interaction interface between ApcD and CP43A1 (Figure 3E,F), which may mediate the energy transfer from ApcD to PSII.
evidence: This is an observation from the surface clip views of the structure.

claim: The interaction interface between ApcD and CP43A1 may mediate the energy transfer from ApcD to PSII.
source: The middle and distal clip views showed an interaction interface between ApcD and CP43A1 (Figure 3E,F), which may mediate the energy transfer from ApcD to PSII.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: Three extra densities not occupied by any model were observed after docking atomic models into the PBS–PSII supercomplex map.
source: After docking the atomic models of PBS, PSII dimer, and two lateral hexamers into the density map of PBS–PSII supercomplex, we still observed three extra densities that are not occupied by any model.
evidence: This is an observation from the model fitting.

claim: Two of the extra densities are associated with the PBS and PSII.
source: Two of them are associated with the PBS and PSII (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and the third one is associated with the lateral hexamer and PSII (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: The third extra density is associated with the lateral hexamer and PSII.
source: Two of them are associated with the PBS and PSII (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and the third one is associated with the lateral hexamer and PSII (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: The three extra densities are temporarily deemed 'connectors' (connectors 1–3).
source: Since we could not identify the proteins corresponding to these densities, we temporarily deemed them 'connectors' (connectors 1–3; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is a naming convention for unidentified densities.

claim: The positions of the connectors in the map suggest that these proteins likely participate in the formation of the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
source: Nevertheless, their positions in the map suggest that these proteins likely participate in the formation of the PBS–PSII supercomplex (Figure 4) as well as the assembling of the PBS–PSII array on the thylakoid membrane (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the positions of the densities.

claim: The connectors likely participate in the assembling of the PBS–PSII array on the thylakoid membrane.
source: Nevertheless, their positions in the map suggest that these proteins likely participate in the formation of the PBS–PSII supercomplex (Figure 4) as well as the assembling of the PBS–PSII array on the thylakoid membrane (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the positions of the densities.

claim: The three connectors are all rod-like structures, but different in size.
source: We segmented out the three connectors from the PBS–PSII supercomplex map and find that they are all rod-like structures, but different in size (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the segmented densities.

claim: Connector 1 contacts the β2 subunit of the PBS core layer a3 and the CP47, D1, and D2 of PSII monomer B2.
source: The surface clip views of connector 1 show that connector 1 contacts the β2 subunit of the PBS core layer a3 and the CP47 of PSII monomer B2 (CP47B2), as well as D1B2 and D2B2 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the surface clip views of the structure.

claim: Connector 2 is smaller than connector 1.
source: Connector 2 is smaller than connector 1 (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a comparison of the sizes of the connectors.

claim: One side of connector 2 interacts with the basal hexamer of Rod a, and the other side with D1B1, D2B1, and CP47B1 in the neighboring PSII monomer B1.
source: One side of connector 2 interacts with the basal hexamer of Rod a, and the other side with D1B1, D2B1, and CP47B1 in the neighboring PSII monomer B1 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the surface clip views of the structure.

claim: Both connector 1 and connector 2 connect with PBS and PSII, suggesting that they may consolidate the anchor of PBS on PSII dimer.
source: Thus, both connector 1 and connector 2 connect with PBS and PSII, suggesting that they may consolidate the anchor of PBS on PSII dimer.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observations.

claim: Connector 3 mediates a connection between the lateral hexamer and the bridging PSII dimer C.
source: Different from connectors 1 and 2, connector 3 mediates a connection between the lateral hexamer and the bridging PSII dimer C.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: Connector 3 could be divided into one small part and one big part.
source: The density map of connector 3 shows that connector 3 could be divided into one small part and one big part (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the density map.

claim: The small part of connector 3 is buried in the lateral hexamer's central cavity, and the big part extends out to connect with PSII.
source: The small part is buried in the lateral hexamer's central cavity, and the big part extends out to connect with PSII.
evidence: This is an observation from the density map.

claim: The structural feature of connector 3 is very similar with the structure of some rod linker proteins, suggesting that connector 3 might be the linker protein of the lateral hexamer.
source: This structural feature is very similar with the structure of some rod linker proteins, such as LR6 of P. purpureum PBS, with the N-terminal rigid domain occupying the central cavity of a hexamer and the C-terminal region extending out, suggesting that connector 3 might be the linker protein of the lateral hexamer.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural similarity.

claim: The lateral hexamer together with connector 3 stabilizes PBS's connection with PSII in the interconnected array of the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
source: The structure indicates that the lateral hexamer together with connector 3 stabilizes PBS's connection with PSII in the interconnected array of the PBS–PSII supercomplex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: PBS is classified into different structural types, including hemidiscoidal, hemiellipsoidal, block type, bundle type and rod type.
source: PBS is classified into different structural types, including hemidiscoidal (Chang et al., 2015), hemiellipsoidal (Arteni et al., 2008), block type (Zhang et al., 2017), bundle type (Guglielmi et al., 1981) and rod type (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hemidiscoidal PBSs of the Synechocystis strain PCC 6803 and the Anabana sp. strain PCC 7120 are associated with one PSII dimer.
source: Hemidiscoidal PBSs of the Synechocystis strain PCC 6803 and the Anabana sp. strain PCC 7120 are associated with one PSII dimer (Chang et al., 2015; Rast et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rod-like AmPBS is composed of four hexamers and is adjacent to one PSII dimer.
source: The rod-like AmPBS is composed of four hexamers and is adjacent to one PSII dimer (Chen et al., 2009; Niedzwiedzki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hemiellipsoidal PBS connects with monomeric PSII at a ratio from 1:1 to 1:4.
source: The hemiellipsoidal PBS connects with monomeric PSII at a ratio from 1:1 to 1:4 (Arteni et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 1989; Lange et al., 1990; Ohki et al., 1987; Takahashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The work reports a different ratio (1:6) of hemiellipsoidal PBS and PSII on the native thylakoid membrane.
source: Using in situ cryo-ET, our work reports the native PBS–PSII supercomplex structure of red algae. The structure reveals a different ratio (1:6) of hemiellipsoidal PBS and PSII on the native thylakoid membrane (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Each PBS directly interacts with two PSII dimers and indirectly interacts with two PSII monomers from two peripheral bridging PSII dimers.
source: Each PBS directly interacts with two PSII dimers and indirectly interacts with two PSII monomers from two peripheral bridging PSII dimers, forming the interconnected array of the PBS–PSII supercomplex with the support of three unassigned connectors.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: With 14° rotation and 30 Å shift of PSII dimer pair relative to PBS core, the terminal emitters, ApcD and αLCM, in the two symmetric a2a3 and a2'a3' hexamers of the core, connect with CP43 of PSII monomers A1 and B2, and CP47 in PSII monomers B1 and A2.
source: With 14° rotation and 30 Å shift of PSII dimer pair relative to PBS core, the terminal emitters, ApcD and αLCM, in the two symmetric a2a3 and a2'a3' hexamers of the core, connect with CP43 of PSII monomers A1 and B2, and CP47 in PSII monomers B1 and A2 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: A similar geometry of the PBS–PSII supercomplex was reported in cyanobacteria and red algae possessing hemidiscoidal PBS.
source: A similar geometry of the PBS–PSII supercomplex was reported in cyanobacteria and red algae possessing hemidiscoidal PBS, suggesting that hemidiscoidal PBSs use the same strategy for energy transfer from PBS to PSII (Arteni et al., 2009; Arteni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hemidiscoidal PBSs use the same strategy for energy transfer from PBS to PSII as hemiellipsoidal PBS.
source: A similar geometry of the PBS–PSII supercomplex was reported in cyanobacteria and red algae possessing hemidiscoidal PBS, suggesting that hemidiscoidal PBSs use the same strategy for energy transfer from PBS to PSII (Arteni et al., 2009; Arteni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity.

claim: The structure enables the extra lateral hexamers in P. purpureum to associate with PSII monomers C1 and C'2 through connector 3.
source: This structure also enables the extra lateral hexamers in P. purpureum to associate with PSII monomers C1 and C'2 through connector 3 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The work focused on the PBS–PSII structures in the ordered distribution regions.
source: In this work, we focused on the PBS–PSII structures in the ordered distribution regions, where both PBS and PSII are neatly arranged according to a strict stoichiometry of 1:6.
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: Previous research conducting fraction freezing analysis has found that the PBS–PSII complexes on random distribution regions could have lower stoichiometry (between 1:1 and 1:4).
source: Previous research conducting fraction freezing analysis (Lange et al., 1990) has found that the PBS–PSII complexes on random distribution regions could have lower stoichiometry (between 1:1 and 1:4), which are represented as an PSII monomer, dimer, trimer, or double dimer.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: These observations show the possible diversity of PBS–PSII organization on the thylakoids.
source: These observations show the possible diversity of PBS–PSII organization on the thylakoids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current and previous observations.

claim: Extensive studies have shown that αLCM and ApcD are the terminal emitters of the energy coupling between PBS and PSII.
source: Extensive studies have shown that αLCM and ApcD are the terminal emitters of the energy coupling between PBS and PSII (Zhao et al., 1992; Zlenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The structures detail the connections of αLCM and ApcD with PSII, which contribute to the energy flows from PBS to PSII.
source: In our structures, we detailed the connections of αLCM and ApcD with PSII, which contribute to the energy flows from PBS to PSII (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: ApcF was reported to be involved in the energy transfer in cyanobacteria.
source: ApcF was also reported to be involved in the energy transfer in cyanobacteria (Calzadilla et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A solid connection between ApcF and PSII could not be found in the structures.
source: However, we could not find a solid connection between ApcF and PSII.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: It is very likely that ApcF only plays an auxiliary role for direct energy transfer to reaction centers in red algae.
source: Thus, it is very likely that ApcF only plays an auxiliary role for direct energy transfer to reaction centers in red algae.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the lack of observed connection.

claim: The molecular weights of the connectors are estimated at around 30–80 kDa according to the size and shape.
source: While the current resolution limited additional detailed analysis of the connectors, we attempted to estimate the molecular weights of these connectors at around 30–80 kDa according to the size and shape (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an estimation based on the structural features.

claim: PSII dimer C does not directly bind to PBS but is closer to the lateral hexamer.
source: We found a class of PSII dimer C (PSII dimer C, C', and C" in Figure 2A) that does not directly bind to PBS but is closer to the lateral hexamer.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: PSII dimer C can only absorb energy from the independent lateral hexamer instead of the whole PBS through connector 3.
source: Since PSII dimer C can only absorb energy from the independent lateral hexamer instead of the whole PBS through connector 3, they could have fewer bilins feeding into them than the other PSIIs and could become saturated with light at higher intensities.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural arrangement.

claim: PSII dimer C could have fewer bilins feeding into them than the other PSIIs and could become saturated with light at higher intensities.
source: Since PSII dimer C can only absorb energy from the independent lateral hexamer instead of the whole PBS through connector 3, they could have fewer bilins feeding into them than the other PSIIs and could become saturated with light at higher intensities.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural arrangement.

claim: If the PSII dimer C is more sensitive to light intensity than the others, it could be involved in the transition between the ordered distribution region and the random distribution region.
source: If the PSII dimer C is more sensitive to light intensity than the others, it could be involved in the transition between the ordered distribution region and the random distribution region.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The energy transfer from PBS to PSII could follow multiple pathways.
source: The energy transfer from PBS to PSII could follow multiple pathways (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The two terminal emitters, αLCM and ApcD, funnel light energy to PSII by distinct structural connections.
source: The two terminal emitters, αLCM and ApcD, funnel light energy to PSII by distinct structural connections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The chromophore of αLCM mediates energy transfer via interaction with CP43 and CP47.
source: The chromophore of αLCM mediates energy transfer via interaction with CP43 and CP47.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The chromophore of ApcD is mediated by interactions with CP43.
source: In contrast, the chromophore of ApcD is mediated by interactions with CP43.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Alternative routes of energy transfer bypassing the PBS core to PSII could exist.
source: Since connector 2 connects with both the basal PC hexamer of Rod a and CP47 of PSII, we speculate that alternative routes of energy transfer bypassing the PBS core to PSII could exist: connector 2 and connector 3 could mediate the energy flow from the basal hexamer of Rod a to PSII and from lateral hexamer to PSII, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural connections.

claim: Connector 2 could mediate the energy flow from the basal hexamer of Rod a to PSII.
source: Since connector 2 connects with both the basal PC hexamer of Rod a and CP47 of PSII, we speculate that alternative routes of energy transfer bypassing the PBS core to PSII could exist: connector 2 and connector 3 could mediate the energy flow from the basal hexamer of Rod a to PSII and from lateral hexamer to PSII, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural connections.

claim: Connector 3 could mediate the energy flow from lateral hexamer to PSII.
source: Since connector 2 connects with both the basal PC hexamer of Rod a and CP47 of PSII, we speculate that alternative routes of energy transfer bypassing the PBS core to PSII could exist: connector 2 and connector 3 could mediate the energy flow from the basal hexamer of Rod a to PSII and from lateral hexamer to PSII, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural connections.

claim: Ueno et al. have reported light energy flows from CP43 to CP47 by energy transfer between the neighboring PSII monomers.
source: Ueno et al. have reported light energy flows from CP43 to CP47 by energy transfer between the neighboring PSII monomers (Ueno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The in situ structure reveals that αLCM transfers energy to CP43 as well as the neighboring CP47, which may suggest that αLCM provides the modulation activity of energy flow between CP43 and the neighboring CP47.
source: Our in situ structure reveals that αLCM transfers energy to CP43 as well as the neighboring CP47, may suggesting that αLCM provides the modulation activity of energy flow between CP43 and the neighboring CP47.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural observations.

claim: It is currently unclear whether the connector proteins play a specific role in the energy transfer between PBS and PSII.
source: However, it is currently unclear whether the connector proteins play a specific role in the energy transfer between PBS and PSII, and this topic requires further study.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and suggests future research.

claim: Thylakoid membrane branching and fusion regions were observed in several tomograms.
source: In several tomograms, we observed the thylakoid membrane branching and fusion regions (Figure 6, Video 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the tomogram data.

claim: The two parallel thylakoid membranes are split into two branches, with one branch approaching and fusing with another branch from the neighboring thylakoid membrane.
source: The two parallel thylakoid membranes are split into two branches. One branch approaches and fuses with another branch from the neighboring thylakoid membrane (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the tomogram data.

claim: The branching and fusing membranes built 'stairs' between two neighboring thylakoid membranes.
source: The 3D segmentation model shows that the branching and fusing membranes built 'stairs' between two neighboring thylakoid membranes (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the 3D segmentation model.

claim: On the top of the 'stairs' is the large perforation on the thylakoids.
source: On the top of the 'stairs' is the large perforation on the thylakoids (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from the 3D segmentation model.

claim: These structures are very similar to the thylakoid membrane architecture in the cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus, Synechococcus sp. PCC 7942 and Microcoleus sp. reported by Nevo et al., 2007.
source: These structures are very similar to the thylakoid membrane architecture in the cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus (Ting et al., 2007), Synechococcus sp. PCC 7942 and Microcoleus sp. reported by Nevo et al., 2007.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies.

claim: Nevo et al. observed perforations as well as branching and fusion of the membranes, which resulted in a highly connected network to allow water-soluble and lipid-soluble molecules to diffuse through the entire membrane network.
source: They also observed perforations as well as branching and fusion of the membranes, which resulted in a highly connected network to allow water-soluble and lipid-soluble molecules to diffuse through the entire membrane network (Nevo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is reasonable to deduce that the perforations and stairs of the thylakoid membrane in the red alga might play the same role as in cyanobacteria.
source: Thus, it is reasonable to deduce that the perforations and stairs of the thylakoid membrane in the red alga might play the same role, although it needs to be further investigated.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural similarity.

claim: The center-to-center distance of two adjacent PBSs is approximately 345 Å.
source: The center-to-center distance of two adjacent PBSs is approximately 345 Å.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 51 cryo-ET tilt series were collected at higher magnification at the ordered distribution regions for 3D reconstruction and further sub-tomogram averaging.
source: Subsequently, 51 cryo-ET tilt series were collected at higher magnification at the ordered distribution regions for three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction and further sub-tomogram averaging.
evidence: This describes the data collection procedure.
